newsitem.title: USA: USAID official slams anti-abortion Republicans.
newsitem.headline: USAID official slams anti-abortion Republicans.

text.p: The Clinton administration's top aid official on Thursday attacked attempts by Republican anti-abortion lawmakers to block a resolution that would speed up U.S. financing to family planning programmes overseas.

"Not one penny of our funding goes to any organisation that breaks the laws of the country in which it operates," Brian Atwood, administrator of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), said in a speech in New York.

"So why then an abortion debate? Maybe the real reason is that the opponents of our funding want to talk about abortion, because they know they can't win a fair discussion on the merits of family planning."

A main congressional opponent of abortion, Representative Chris Smith of New Jersey, was quoted by the New York Times Thursday as saying he has enough votes in the House to pass a ban on federal money for groups that perform abortions overseas, even if they were using private money.
The measure would reimpose a ban by the Reagan and Bush administrations that President Clinton lifted by executive order when he took office four years ago.

Smith has promoted the measure as an alternative to an administration-supported proposal that would release funds already appropriated for family planning in 1997 on March 1 rather than being held up until July.
If the money is made available in March, it would amount to $215 million but be reduced to $92 million if left until July.
Both measures could be voted on as early as next week.

Congress last year voted to reduce money for international family planning programmes by 35 percent and prevent any further spending until July 1. It established a system to allow only part of the $385 million appropriated to be spent each month.

Atwood told a meeting co-sponsored by the Columbia School of Public Health and the Rockefeller Foundation that USAID opposes policies such as China involuntarily imposing population control as well as "those who would deny women access to family planning services."
He said the Reagan and Bush policy had denied USAID the right to work with "some of the most effective family planning organisations in the world."

President Clinton has said that to delay spending would deny safe and effective contraception to couples who depend on these programmes and would lead to "a rise in unintended pregnancies and maternal deaths and a tragic recourse to unsafe and unsanitary methods to terminate those pregnancies."

Abortion opponents such as the National Conference of Catholic Bishops said the programmes amount to "exporting abortions to developing nations" because the money goes to organisations that perform abortions in those countries.
